power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To develop a preliminary approach for identifying individuals with stroke exhibiting arm nonuse, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to evaluate how well paretic arm choice during the Complex Grasp condition distinguished individuals who showed nonuse on the AAUT from those who did not show nonuse on the AAUT, based on the AAUT Nonuse Index. Although there is no "gold standard" for determining nonuse, we used the published AAUT Nonuse Index as the reference measure, with values >0.5 classified as nonuse and values ≤0.5 classified as no nonuse, based on a threshold employed in previous work. 9 The proportion of paretic arm choice in the Complex Grasp condition was entered as the continuous predictor, with AAUT-defined nonuse status as the binary outcome. Discriminative ability was quantified using the area under the curve (AUC). An exploratory threshold for paretic arm choice was selected by maximizing sensitivity and specificity (Youden's index; sensitivity + specificity -1). 42 Because the threshold was derived from the present sample, it was considered preliminary and requires independent validation. The present study was conducted as part of a broader, multi-aim study, and no formal a priori power analysis was conducted specifically for these validation analyses. Sample size was determined by balancing feasibility considerations with the goal of completing this phase of tool development and making the VR-NonUse tool available for further evaluation in a timely manner. Post hoc sensitivity analyses were conducted to characterize the statistical sensitivity of the study design. For the correlation-based validity analyses, an approximate sensitivity analysis Virtual reality for assessment of nonuse was conducted using the sample of 51 participants with stroke, a two-sided α=.05, and 80% power. 43 For the mixed-effects construct-validity analysis, simulation-based sensitivity analyses were conducted using the fitted linear mixed-effects model as the data-generating model. 44, 45 The model included fixed effects of Group, Condition, and the Group × Condition interaction and a random intercept for participant. Fixed-effect estimates and variance components from the model fitted to the full observed sample were held constant across simulations. We varied the number of simulated participants (N=30, 40, 50, 60, and 74) to examine how power changed with sample size, while approximately preserving the observed group composition and repeated-trial structure. For each sample size, 1,000 datasets were simulated and analyzed using the same linear mixed-effects model as the primary analysis. Estimated marginal condition means and Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons were then used to evaluate the cognitive-demand contrast (Basic Grasp vs. Complex Grasp) and motor-demand contrast (Complex Grasp vs. Complex Point). Power was estimated as the proportion of simulated datasets in which the respective comparison yielded p<.05. Because these analyses were conducted post hoc and incorporated effect estimates and variance components obtained from the observed data, they were interpreted as descriptive assessments of sensitivity to effects of the magnitude observed in the present sample rather than as retrospective justification of the original sample size.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. live_data_statements: Fifty-one right-handed individuals with stroke (29 left cerebrovascular accident (LCVA); 22 right cerebrovascular accident (RCVA); 18 females, mean age=60.4±12.1 years; time post-stroke=67.6±67.9 months) and 23 age-matched right-handed Virtual reality for assessment of nonuse neurotypical individuals (12 females, mean age=64.4±12.6 years) were recruited from the Neurocognitive Rehabilitation Research Registry at Moss Rehabilitation Research Institute. 25 Inclusion criteria were age 18-90 years and the ability to provide informed consent.
Specifically, potential participants were asked about their previous VR experiences and whether they had experienced discomfort or other adverse effects during VR exposure.
Control participants were excluded for cognitive impairment (Montreal Cognitive Assessment score <16). 26 Participant demographics and behavioral assessment scores are shown in Table 1.
Performance was video recorded throughout; participants were unaware of the recording during the spontaneous condition and were debriefed after the assessment.
Prior to the assessment, participants were familiarized with the target objects.

Participants were instructed to reach toward previously familiarized objects presented on three shelves of a virtual shelving unit located ~60cm in front of the lap tray (adjusted for participants' arm length), subtended ~66.7° of visual angle, with shelves positioned 6, 21, and 36cm above the lap tray.
Participants were instructed to touch the four corners of the virtual shelf and to reach to a ball presented at each target location to confirm they could reach all possible locations with both arms.
Participants completed 10 practice trials involving reaching with either arm to point or grasp target objects among semantically related distractors.

Participants had 7000ms to locate and touch or grasp the target object. 15, 28 Before each condition, participants were instructed to freely choose either arm to reach and poke or grasp to lift the target object and to complete the task as quickly and accurately as possible.
Participants were tested under three conditions.

At Visit 1, participants completed the AAUT, along with measures of stroke severity (NIH Stroke Scale) and a measure of lateralized and non-lateralized visual attention (Virtual Reality Lateralized Attention Test-2; VRLAT-2), that shows evidence of moderate discriminant and concurrent validity. 31, 32 Visit 2 included sensorimotor assessments.

During Visits 3-5/6, all participants completed the 6-block VR-NonUse assessment (two blocks x three conditions), performing 2 or 3 blocks per session according to their assigned randomization sequence.
Control participants completed 2-3 sessions that included the VRLAT and the VR-NonUse assessment.

Stroke participants were labeled by lesioned hemisphere based on evidence indicating hemispheric differences in paretic arm use. 15, 38 The assumption of homogeneity of variance was evaluated by examining model residuals for evidence of systematic changes in residual variance across fitted values and experimental groups/conditions.
All included participants completed the VR-NonUse assessment across the scheduled study visits.
All participants completed the assessment without difficulty.

First, the study was conducted as part of a larger research project and was not prospectively designed, analyzed, or interpreted according to Consensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) recommendations. 60 Second, participants were required to demonstrate a minimum level of upper-extremity motor function, and there were relatively few subjects in the range of moderate impairment.
Consent to participate: Participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the Institutional Review Board of Thomas Jefferson University.
